QUESTION OF THE WEEK - After Q1 GDP data last week showed annual growth slowing to a five year low of 2.4 percent we asked analysts their expectations for GDP growth in 1997/98.
The government forecast 3.75 percent in its budget and the Reserve Bank has talked about 4.0 percent, the minimum growth rate necessary to make inroads into unemployment.
From the range of responses it seems the market is a lot less certain than the central bank that such growth is attainable.
Of the 25 economists surveyed, 13 thought growth would fall short while nine were clustered at four or just above and a handful saw prospects for a substantially better outcome.
That gave a median of 3.9 percent which, while hardly scientific, does suggest the risks of overshooting are less than those of falling short, so the RBA would be sensible to keep an easing bias.
Housing Employment Unemployment Part rate GDP

HOUSING FINANCE - Analysts say private data on commitments from the major banks show strong growth in April with a raw rise of around 15 percent. The mortgage originators are unlikely to have done much worse so most were confident of calling a rise of at least 10 percent for overall commitments. Such a result would confirm the upbeat outlook for housing the market had held for some time now and suggest housing will increasingly contribute to GDP growth in 1997/98 after detracting in the last year or two. The future should have been further brightened by the official rate cut of May 23 which saw mortgage rates down to 20-year lows. Greater demand for housing usually translates into increased demand for household goods, which promises to help retail sales recover from April's shock 1.7 percent plunge.

EMPLOYMENT - Weakness in jobs growth and the stubbornly high level of unemployment has been a major driving force in the four rate cuts the RBA has delivered since last July, which makes this data of crucial importance to the markets. A weak result would almost certainly see pressure build for another easing, while a big rise in employment would increase the chance of policy staying steady in the foreseeable future. The breakdown between part time and full time employment would also be important since most of what gains there have been in the past year were concentrated in the former, which neither pay as much nor are as secure as full time jobs.
